sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Mixcōātl** (*mixcoatl*) — Clouds, Hunting, the Milky Way · "Cloud Serpent" — god of the hunt, of clouds, and of the starry road — belongs to the Nahuatl tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Clouds, Hunting, the Milky Way". The name means ""Cloud Serpent" — god of the hunt, of clouds, and of the starry road"[^1].

Mixcōātl is the Aztec god of the hunt and the starry road: the cloud-serpent who slides along the Milky Way, patron of the nomadic hunters who became the Aztecs' ancestors — the oldest god of the road that leads to the empire.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Mixcōātl** and serves its temple at [mixcōātl.com](https://xn--mixctl-6za12d.com). The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *mixcoatl* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No indigenous written attestation survives for this name; **Mixcōātl** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means ""Cloud Serpent" — god of the hunt, of clouds, and of the starry road"[^1].

The ASCII form *mixcoatl* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Mixcōātl** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **m** → **M** — Same
- **i** → **i** — Same
- **x** → **x** — Same
- **c** → **c** — Same
- **o** → **ō** — Long ō of cōātl
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **t** → **t** — Same
- **l** → **l** — Same

The project holds the domain **mixcōātl.com** (xn--mixctl-6za12d.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain), Bernardino de Sahagún; School of American Research, 1577.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/miʃ.ˈkoː.aː.tɬ/** — Classical Nahuatl.[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: meesh-KOH-ahtl — long o, lateral finish.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Nahuatl** — Mixcōātl
- **His other name** — Camaxtle
- **Owned form** — Mixcōātl

Mixcōātl is Nahuatl for "cloud serpent" (mixtli + cōātl); the macron on the ō marks the long vowel of the serpent-word, the same one in Quetzalcōātl and Xōlōtl. The restoration keeps it — the serpent is always long. The x of Nahuatl is the sh-sound, not ks: meesh, not mix — the single most misread letter in the language.

sources.citation: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain), Bernardino de Sahagún; School of American Research, 1577.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
No indigenous writing system is securely attested for individual nahuatl names. The form shown is a modern scholarly transliteration.[^1]

The form **Mixcōātl** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

sources.citation: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain), Bernardino de Sahagún; School of American Research, 1577.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Mixcōātl is the Aztec god of the hunt and the starry road: the cloud-serpent who slides along the Milky Way, patron of the nomadic hunters who became the Aztecs' ancestors — the oldest god of the road that leads to the empire.[^1]

### The Milky Way

His body in the sky: the star-serpent, the road of the night.

### The Hunt

Patron of hunters — his bow and net, the Chichimec tool-kit.

### The Cloud

The weather-serpent: rain and sky in motion.

### Camaxtle

His other name — the ancient hunting god of the Chichimecs.

sources.citation: Bernardino de Sahagún, Florentine Codex, General History of the Things of New Spain, 1577.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Mixcōātl concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The bow and arrows** — The hunt — his gift to the wandering tribes
- **The star-serpent** — The Milky Way as a living road
- **The white stripes** — His hunting-paint, cloud on dark sky

sources.citation: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain), Bernardino de Sahagún; School of American Research, 1577.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Mixcōātl's myths are the Aztec origin-story in one figure: the wilderness god who taught the city-builders how to hunt, and whose star-road they followed south.[^1]

### The Serpent of Stars (The Road)

The Chichimec tribes who became the Aztec nobility followed his road: the Milky Way, which the Nahuatl called Mixcōātl, the Cloud Serpent, slithering nightly across the sky. The migrating peoples read their path in his body — the desert crossed by the serpent's light — and when they founded Tenochtitlan, they enthroned the wilderness-guide among the city's great gods, the god of where they had come from.[^2]

### The Bow of the Chichimecs (The Gift)

As Camaxtle, he gave the wandering tribes the bow and the fire-drill — the two technologies of the road. The Aztec coronation rites remembered: the new Tlatoani dressed as Mixcōātl for the warrior's investiture, and the festival of Quecholli ("the precious feather") honored him with the hunt's own weapons laid on his altar — the city's annual thanks to the god who fed it before it had fields.

### Father of the Four Hundred (The Father)

The myth makes him father of the Centzon Huitznāhua — the Four Hundred Southerners, the star-host whom Coyolxāuhqui led against their mother when she bore Huitzilopochtli. The god of the hunt is thus also the father of the enemies of the sun: the Aztec sky-war between day and night is, in his household, a family quarrel, written nightly across his own starry body.

sources.citation: Bernardino de Sahagún, Florentine Codex, General History of the Things of New Spain, 1577.
Frances Karttunen, An Analytical Dictionary of Nahuatl, University of Texas Press, 1983.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
The hunt-gods of North America stand in his lineage: the Huichol's Kauyumari (the blue deer-guide) and the Maya hunting-lords share his road-and-prey theology. Colonial chroniclers merged him with Santiago and with Nimrod (the hunter-king of the missionaries' Genesis); the people kept the star-serpent — and hunters in rural Mexico still note the sky's deer-road on the way to the field.[^1]

Within the Nahuatl tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[cihuacoatl|Cihuacōātl]], [[coatlicue|Cōātlīcue]], [[huitzilopochtli|Huitzilopōchtli]], [[itzpapalotl|Itzpapālōtl]], [[mictlantecutli|Mictlāntēcutli]], and [[quetzalcoatl|Quetzalcōātl]].

sources.citation: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain), Bernardino de Sahagún; School of American Research, 1577.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: His name survives in the Milky Way's Nahuatl name itself; the Quecholli weapons-festival is documented in the Florentine Codex's fullest ritual detail; and the Chichimec hunting mythology is the standard account of the Aztecs' own self-image: the empire that began as wanderers following a serpent of stars. The Mexican National Museum of Anthropology's Mixcōātl figures — striped, netted, bowed — are his standing portraits.[^1]

sources.citation: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain), Bernardino de Sahagún; School of American Research, 1577.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: Teotihuacan's hunting-god precedes him; the Toltec-Aztec Camaxtle cult at Tula and the Templo Mayor's offerings (his arrows among the buried gifts) anchor his archaeology. The Florentine Codex's Quecholli chapter — weapons, dance, and the hunt's liturgy — is the fullest record, and the rock-art of the northern deserts (the bowmen of the Sierra Madre) keeps his people's original ground.[^1]

sources.citation: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain), Bernardino de Sahagún; School of American Research, 1577.

sections.label: Florentine Codex
sections.body: Sahagún's Codex gives him the hunter's chapter: Mixcōātl, "Cloud Serpent," god of the hunt and of the Milky Way, whose festival **Quecholli** ("the precious feather") honored him with the laying of weapons on his altar. The Codex's account of the Tlatoani's investiture shows the new king dressed as Mixcōātl for the warrior rites — the empire formally dressed as the wilderness that made it.

sources.citation: Florentine Codex, Books 1, 2 (Quecholli), 8 (investiture).

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Aztec Sources
sections.body: The migration traditions make him the road-god: the Chichimec ancestors followed his star-road south — the Milky Way as the Cloud Serpent's body — and the Codex Boturini's itinerary places the hunt-god's cult at every stage of the walk to Tenochtitlan. The Leyenda de los Soles makes him father of the Centzon Huitznāhua, the star-host of the night sky's war.

sources.citation: Codex Boturini (migration); Leyenda de los Soles.

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Colonial-Era Sources
sections.body: The chroniclers filed him under two wrong names — Nimrod the hunter-king and Santiago Matamoros — and the people kept the serpent: Durán describes the Quecholli weapons-dance and the hunters' guilds; the relaciones of the northern provinces record the Camaxtle-cult among the Chichimec-speaking peoples. The colonial record's value is the proof of continuity: the hunt-god outlived the hunt, and his star-road is still read in the Sierra Madre's night.

sources.citation: Durán (Quecholli); the northern relaciones (Camaxtle).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Mixcōātl is the god of the journey that made you. Every settled people remembers, somewhere, the road: the serpent in the night sky that was followed here. He asks the traveler's question, which is also the nation's and the individual's: what star did your ancestors follow — and does it still move, when you look up, the way it moved for them?

The weapons on his altar were the archaeology of gratitude: the city laid its old tools down each year, remembering what fed it first. Every settled people owes a debt to its wilderness; the Aztecs paid theirs honestly, in bows, once a year, to the serpent in the clouds.

The Chichimec road is still walked, in a way: every migrant moving north across the same deserts reads the same sky. The serpent of stars has not moved; it is the walkers who change. Mixcōātl's question outlasted his temples: not what you hunt, but what star you follow — and whether you thank it when you arrive.

The Florentine Codex keeps the festival's strangest detail: the king himself dressed as the hunt-god, net and all, at the year's darkest rite — the empire's ruler periodically reminded, in costume, that his house began as wanderers. Every nation needs that costume somewhere in its closet: the reminder of the road, worn by the people who have forgotten it most.

Look up on a dry winter night from the same deserts his people crossed: the serpent still pours itself across the sky, head south, tail north, the oldest road sign in the hemisphere. The empires built on his route are dust in his direction, and the migrants still walking it are his living congregation — the hunt, the road, the star, unchanged.[^1]

sources.citation: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain), Bernardino de Sahagún; School of American Research, 1577.
